segments.t: Still in the mayor's office, a moment later. Last time, Samson, the bully from Arkady's childhood, came to ask for a better job, and Arkady talked him into phoning his boss and quitting on the spot. Now Samson wants to know when he starts, and Arkady has one small condition. We'll hear it in Russian first; don't worry about catching every word.
Аркаш, ну что скажешь? Когда начинать?
Я тебе тогда сказал: ты меня ещё поцелуешь.
Не надо, Самсон. Сейчас придёт охрана.
Let's go back through it. Samson has just quit his old job, so he is in a hurry to start the new one.
'Arkasha, so what do you say?' He uses a short, friendly form of Arkady's name, as old neighbours do.
'When do I start?' Literally, 'when to start?' Just the word for 'when' and a verb in its basic form. Arkady is all smiles.
'Any time you like.' Literally, 'at any moment'. Samson doesn't need to be asked twice.
'Right, I'm ready!' The first word means 'all', but here it just means 'that's settled'. Then Arkady slips in one more thing.
'There's just one small formality.' The long word sounds just like its English cousin. Samson is puzzled.
'What formality?' The question word changes its ending to match the feminine noun. Arkady's answer is short.
'Kiss me.' This is the command form of the verb 'to kiss'. In the show he names a crude, humiliating kind of kiss; we keep it simple. Samson can't believe his ears.
'What?' A casual, rather rough way to say it. So Arkady reminds him of their childhood.

'Do you remember the toilet in the communal flat?' When they were boys, Samson used to push little Arkasha's head into that toilet. Notice that the endings change after the little word for 'in'. And the boy made a promise.
Я тебе тогда сказал: ты меня ещё поцелуешь.
'I told you back then: you'll kiss me one day.' The verb for 'told' is past tense and masculine, because Arkady is a man. Samson is amazed.
'What, you remember all that?' Arkady's answer is the line he has waited thirty years to say.
'Oh, I remember everything.' The little word at the start, meaning 'and' or 'but', gives it a quiet, calm sting. Samson hopes it's a joke.
'Are you joking?' But Arkady keeps a straight face.
'No. I'm serious.' A phrase Arkady likes; you'll hear it from him again. Samson explodes.
'No! Never!' He is furious and comes at Arkady, who doesn't even get up.
Не надо, Самсон. Сейчас придёт охрана.
'Don't, Samson. Security will be here any second.' Two very useful words open this line: they mean 'don't' or 'no need'. And the guards do come in.
'Please see him out.' To the guards Arkady is polite, so the verb has the formal, plural ending. And as Samson leaves, one last line.
'If you change your mind, come back.' There is no word for 'if': the first verb, in the future, does that job.
'The job is waiting.' The word here means a post, a position, rather than simple work. Let's listen to the whole scene once more.
Аркаш, ну что скажешь? Когда начинать?
Я тебе тогда сказал: ты меня ещё поцелуешь.
Не надо, Самсон. Сейчас придёт охрана.
That's it for this part: a childhood promise, kept after thirty years. When you watch the episode, listen for Arkady's calm reply about remembering everything; you'll catch it now. See you next time.
